VOL. 1 · NO. 1 MEDIA LITERACY EDITION PRICE: YOUR ATTENTION

Read Between
the Lines

Fact · Opinion · Verification · How News Gets Shaped

The most confusing media is usually not totally fake. It is real facts, real photos, and real quotes, arranged to push you toward a feeling before you have enough evidence.

A Field Guide for Readers in Grades 5 to 7
↓   Scroll to investigate   ↓
Chapter One

Everything Is a Message

Media is any way people send a message to other people. It is not just "the news."

A newspaper is media. So is a TikTok, a podcast, a meme, a movie trailer, a campaign poster, a cereal box, a search result, and a text from your friend. If something is trying to communicate, it is media. That means somebody made it, somebody had a reason, and somebody made choices about how it would look and sound.

Being media literate does not mean trusting everything. It also does not mean doubting everything. It means asking better questions. The National Association for Media Literacy Education describes media literacy as the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create, and act using all kinds of communication.

Stop & Think

Imagine a school basketball game. One report says: "The Tigers beat the Bulldogs 42 to 38." Another says: "The Tigers absolutely crushed the Bulldogs because we are obviously the best team in the county." Both are media. What is the difference between them?

The first one is checkable. You could look up the score. The second one mixes a fact (a win happened) with strong opinion ("absolutely crushed," "obviously the best") and exaggeration. Same event, very different message.
Chapter Two

Fact, Opinion,
and the Blur

A fact is checkable

A fact is a statement that can be checked against evidence. A fact can turn out true or false, but the point is that you can test it. "The game started at 6:00 p.m." and "The video has 2 million views" are facts because records, photos, or witnesses could confirm them.

Careful: a sentence is not true just because it sounds factual. "Scientists proved that eating chocolate every day makes you smarter" sounds like a fact, but before believing it you would ask which scientists, what study, how many people, and whether the headline is exaggerating. A fact must be checkable. A verified fact has actually been checked.

An opinion is a judgment

An opinion is a belief, feeling, or interpretation. Opinions can be smart or silly, supported or unsupported, but they cannot be proven the way a simple fact can. Watch for words like best, worst, should, unfair, amazing, boring, dangerous, and terrible. These words are not bad, but they signal that someone is making a judgment.

Many sentences mix both

Here is the tricky part. Real media often packs fact and opinion into one sentence:

The sentence

"The school board voted 5 to 2 to approve the new dress code, a disappointing decision that ignores student voices."

The factual core

The school board voted 5 to 2 to approve the new dress code. That is checkable.

The opinion mixed in

"A disappointing decision that ignores student voices" is a judgment. You could argue about it, but you cannot prove it like a vote count.

Quick Check
Which sentence is a pure FACT (no opinion mixed in)?
Correct. "The city opened a new skate park on Monday" can be checked against records and reporting. The other two sneak in judgments like "best" and "wasted."
Not quite. Look for the sentence with no judgment words. "Best" and "wasted" are opinions. The checkable one is: the city opened a new skate park on Monday.
Chapter Three

The Third Thing: Analysis

Between plain fact and plain opinion sits a third thing. It explains what the facts might mean.

Analysis combines facts, background knowledge, and careful interpretation. Watch how the same situation produces three different kinds of statements:

Fact

The team lost three games in a row.

Opinion

The team is awful.

Analysis

The team has lost three games in a row, partly because two starting players are injured and the defense has allowed more points than earlier in the season.

Good analysis is built on evidence. Weak analysis jumps to conclusions. News organizations publish straight news, analysis, opinion columns, and editorials, and responsible ones label which is which. The Society of Professional Journalists says journalists should verify information, use original sources, provide context, and clearly label commentary and advocacy.

Chapter Four

Not Every "Article"
Is the Same Thing

On one news website you might find a straight news story, a feature, an investigation, an analysis, an opinion column, an editorial, a letter to the editor, and an advertisement dressed up to look like a story. Each has a different job. Knowing the job tells you how to read it.

Opinion shows are media too

Television and online "commentary" shows are mostly opinion and analysis, not straight news, even when they cover real events. Hosts pick a topic, choose an angle, and tell you how they feel about it. That is allowed. The skill is recognizing it.

Notice that these examples lean in different political directions. That is the point. Opinion content is not a "one side" thing. Strong framing, dramatic music, and emotional language show up on the left, the right, and everywhere in between. Your job is the same no matter who is talking: find the factual core, then decide for yourself.

Quick Check
A TV host spends ten minutes explaining why a new law is "a disaster." This is mostly:
Right. A real topic plus a host's judgment ("a disaster") is opinion and analysis. Being on a news channel or sounding confident does not turn it into straight news.
Look again. The word "disaster" is a judgment. The host is sharing an opinion and analysis about a real law, not delivering neutral news.
Chapter Five

Assets: The Building Blocks

An asset is a piece of material used to build or support a story.

Think of a news story like a school project. The assets are the materials: photos, videos, audio clips, documents, screenshots, maps, charts, data tables, interview recordings, social posts, public records, and satellite images. A story about a storm might use a flood photo, a video of rain, a weather alert, a resident interview, a map, and power outage data.

Here is the rule that trips most people up. An asset is not automatically proof. A photo can be real but old. A video can be real but from a different place. A screenshot can be edited. A quote can be taken out of context. That is exactly why verification matters.

Stop & Think

Someone posts a real photo of a crowded hospital with the caption "This is happening in OUR town RIGHT NOW." The photo is genuine. What could still be wrong?

The photo could be real but from a different city, or from years ago. The asset is real, but the claim attached to it (here, now, our town) might be false. Always ask not only "Is this image real?" but "Is this image being used honestly?"
Chapter Six

When a Real Video
Tells a Lie

Photos and videos feel powerful because they look like direct proof. But a clip can mislead if it is cropped, slowed down, sped up, started too late, ended too early, or given a caption that tells you what to think before you watch. People sometimes call these misleading clips cheapfakes, because they do not need fancy technology. They just need a pair of scissors and a misleading caption.

The clip was real. The footage was not faked. What changed the meaning was removing the context: the parts before and after, and the wider camera angle. Misleading clips like this have spread about politicians of every party.

Questions to ask any clip

What happens right before the clip starts? What happens right after it ends? Is there wider footage from another angle? Who posted it first? And is the caption quietly telling you what to conclude?

Quick Check
A 4-second clip seems to show a politician acting strangely. The best next move is to:
Exactly. Finding the full footage and the original poster is how you catch a clip taken out of context.
Think about the G7 example. The clip was real but misleading. The smart move is to find the longer, wider video and the original source before believing or sharing.
Chapter Seven

The Verification Ladder

Picture a ladder. The higher you climb, the stronger the evidence gets.

Imagine a claim spreads: "The bridge collapsed." How much should you believe it? It depends on the evidence behind it.

1
Someone said it. "People online are saying the bridge collapsed." This is weak. It might just be rumor.
2
A screenshot claims it. Screenshots can be fake, edited, or missing context.
3
A named person claims it. Better, but one person can still be mistaken.
4
A credible organization reports it, and explains how it knows. Stronger.
5
The original source confirms it. "The city transportation department confirmed the bridge closed at 3:15 p.m." Strong.
6
Multiple independent sources confirm it with original evidence. Very strong.
A claim gets stronger when it has a named source, a date, a location, original evidence, multiple independent confirmations, clear context, and a correction if something was wrong earlier.Based on standards from the Associated Press and the Society of Professional Journalists
Chapter Eight

Four Moves: SIFT

When something grabs your attention online, run the SIFT moves. They are quick, and they work.

S

Stop

Pause before reacting or sharing. Is this trying to make you angry, scared, or excited? Do you even know where it came from?

I

Investigate the source

Who made this? A newsroom, a government agency, an expert, an advertiser, an activist group, a random account, or a bot?

F

Find better coverage

Are other reliable sources reporting the same thing? Can you find the original document, full video, or data?

T

Trace to the original

Where did the claim first appear? Is the quote complete? Is the image old? Is the headline exaggerating the study?

SIFT was developed by media educator Mike Caulfield and is taught in digital literacy programs everywhere. The middle two moves point you toward a habit so useful it has its own name.

Chapter Nine

Read Sideways,
Not Just Down

Lateral reading means opening new tabs to see what other sources say about a claim or website, instead of only staring at the page you landed on. Reading "down" a single page (its logo, its About page, its fancy design) is called vertical reading, and it is not enough, because a fake or biased site can look completely professional.

The Digital Inquiry Group, which grew out of research at Stanford, teaches that checking what other websites say about a source usually beats trusting what the source says about itself.

Try It

You see a post: "A new law says students must attend school on Saturdays. Share now!" What do you check, and where?

Do not just read the post. Open new tabs: check your school district website, your state education department, and local news. Search the exact claim. Look for the original law or announcement. If no real source backs it up, do not share it.

The Three-Question Test

Before believing or sharing anything, ask: Who is behind this? What is the evidence? What do other reliable sources say? Three questions, every time.

Chapter Ten

News Is Built
From Choices

A news story is not a random pile of facts. It is shaped by decisions. That is not automatically dishonest. But it always matters.

Watch how the very same event can be framed many ways. A school starts a no-phone policy. Every headline below could be true, yet each one points your attention somewhere different:

Angle: students

"Students adjust to new no-phone rule"

Angle: teachers

"Teachers say phone ban improves attention"

Angle: parents

"Parents question emergency access under new policy"

Angle: discipline data

"School says discipline referrals dropped after phone ban"

Editors also choose what to cover, who to quote, which facts to include or leave out, what words to use, which image to run, and what headline to write. Compare a neutral and a loaded version of one sentence:

Neutral

The mayor said the plan would reduce traffic.

Loaded

The mayor bragged that his plan would magically fix traffic.

"Bragged" and "magically" push you toward eye-rolling before you have heard a single fact. And remember headlines: many people read only the headline. "Study finds link between sleep and test scores" is careful. "Scientists prove sleeping more makes you a genius" exaggerates the same study.

Quick Check
Two true headlines describe the same vote. Which one is shaping your feelings more strongly?
Yes. "Greedy," "waste," and "nobody asked for" are loaded judgments stacked onto the same basic fact.
Compare the word choices. "Greedy," "waste," and "nobody asked for" are judgments. The first headline just states the action and the cost.
Chapter Eleven

Bias Does Not
Always Mean Lying

Bias means a tendency, preference, or leaning. It can show up through which stories get picked, which words and images are used, which sources get quoted, and what context is included or left out. Bias is not always on purpose. A reporter trying to be fair can still miss a viewpoint. A student writing about a school rule might only interview friends who agree with them.

Charts like this can start a useful conversation, but treat them as a starting point, not the final word. The honest goal is not to hunt for a perfectly bias-free human, because there is no such thing. The goal is to notice how a message is shaped so you can think for yourself.

Chapter Twelve

Who Checks
the Claims?

Some organizations exist mainly to test specific public claims and rate how accurate they are. Done well, this kind of fact-checking is transparent and nonpartisan, meaning it does not pick a team. The International Fact-Checking Network publishes a code of principles for exactly this reason.

You will also see platforms attach labels to posts. A label like the one below flags a claim as misleading and points to evidence. Labels can be helpful, but you should still trace the claim yourself.

Watch for the difference between a claim and a judgment. "This post was fact-checked" is a fact. "Therefore everything that source ever says is a lie" is an overstatement. One check is about one claim.
Chapter Thirteen

A Correction Is
a Good Sign

It might seem backwards, but a news source that publishes corrections is showing responsibility, not weakness. Owning a mistake and fixing the record is one of the green flags of trustworthy journalism.

So when you are sizing up a source, do not just ask whether it has ever been wrong. Everyone is sometimes wrong. Ask whether it tells you when it was wrong, and fixes it.

Chapter Fourteen

Three Words
People Mix Up

These words are related, but they are not the same, and the difference is usually about intent and emotion.

Misinformation

False or misleading information shared without meaning to cause harm. Example: a student reshares an old flood photo, honestly thinking it happened today. Tap misinformation.

Disinformation

False or misleading information spread on purpose. Example: someone knowingly posts a fake school-closing notice to trick people. Tap disinformation.

Propaganda

Information designed to influence beliefs or actions, often using emotion, repetition, symbols, and enemy images. It can even contain true facts. Tap propaganda.

Propaganda is worth a closer look, because some of the most famous examples in history were made by governments using real events and very real emotions. That is where our field trip into the past begins.

◊ ◊ ◊
History File One · 1898

Yellow Journalism
and the Maine

In the late 1800s, publishers Joseph Pulitzer and William Randolph Hearst fought for readers with giant headlines, dramatic drawings, and emotional stories. This style got a nickname: yellow journalism.

When the U.S. battleship Maine exploded in Havana Harbor in 1898, the real cause was not yet known. But some papers printed certainty anyway, blaming Spain in enormous type and offering rewards, before any investigation was finished.

The U.S. State Department's history office notes that this coverage sometimes included rousing stories that turned out to be false, using bold headlines and creative drawings to sell papers. The lesson for a modern reader: a story can be built on a real event and still be shaped in a misleading way. Big type and a dramatic picture are not the same as evidence.

Quick Check
What was the main problem with the "Spain Guilty!" headline?
Right. The explosion was real, but the certainty was not earned yet. The headline presented an unproven claim as settled fact.
The explosion really happened, and big type is allowed. The real problem was printing a confident verdict before the cause had been investigated.
History File Two · World War I

Posters With
a Mission

During World War I, the U.S. government created the Committee on Public Information to build public support for the war. The Library of Congress describes it as a sweeping propaganda campaign that shaped opinion through posters, films, and speeches. The facts were real: the country was at war and needed soldiers, money, and supplies. But the messages were designed to persuade, not just to inform.

Look at the techniques, not just the topic. A direct stare, a pointing finger, the word "you," a feeling of guilt or duty. These are emotional tools. A government message can contain true facts and still be carefully engineered to move your feelings and your behavior.

History File Three · World War II

Pride, Fear,
and Persuasion

World War II posters urged Americans to buy war bonds, conserve resources, join the service, and guard their words. The National Archives exhibit "Powers of Persuasion" explains how these posters used form and content to move people to action, through pride, fear, guilt, and patriotic imagery.

A message can support a genuine goal and still use emotional persuasion. Both things are true at once. That is exactly why a careful reader separates the information ("careless talk can be risky") from the persuasion (the fear, the slogan, the dramatic picture).

History File Four · 1938

The Myth About
the Myth

In 1938, Orson Welles aired a radio drama of The War of the Worlds using a realistic news-bulletin style. The famous story is that millions of Americans panicked, sure that aliens were invading.

Here is the twist. Historians now argue that the mass panic was greatly exaggerated, partly by newspapers that had their own reasons to make radio look dangerous. So we have a media event (the broadcast) wrapped inside a media myth (the giant panic) that itself needs fact-checking.

Stop & Think

Why might 1938 newspapers want to exaggerate how badly radio "fooled" everyone?

Radio was a new competitor for people's attention and for advertising money. Making the rival medium look reckless and dangerous served the newspapers' interests. The lesson: even the story about a media event can be shaped by who is telling it and what they gain.
Chapter Nineteen

Ads Wearing
a Disguise

Some online content is an advertisement designed to look like a regular article. This is called sponsored content or native advertising. The Federal Trade Commission says ads must not mislead people about being ads, and that people should be able to tell it is advertising before they click in.

Train your eyes to spot the small print: Sponsored, Advertisement, Paid post, Partner content, Presented by, or Promoted. A headline like "Five reasons this energy drink will change your school day" is doing the job of an ad, even if it is shaped like a story.

Quick Check
You find an article that looks normal but has a small "Sponsored" tag at the top. It is mostly:
Correct. The "Sponsored" label is the tell. Its real job is to promote a product, no matter how article-like it looks.
Look at that "Sponsored" tag. It signals advertising. The article shape is a disguise for a promotion.
Chapter Twenty

Flags to Watch For

A red flag does not prove something is false. It means slow down. A green flag does not prove something is true. It means the source is showing signs of responsibility. Use them as signals, not as final verdicts.

Red Flags

  • "They don't want you to know this"
  • "Share before it's deleted"
  • "100% proof" or "everyone is lying"
  • No source, no date, no author
  • A cropped video or a screenshot with no link
  • ALL CAPS and emotional music
  • Headline does not match the article
  • An old photo presented as new

Green Flags

  • A clear author and a clear date
  • Links to original documents
  • Named sources and multiple viewpoints
  • Clearly labels opinion and analysis
  • Explains what is still unknown
  • Avoids exaggerated certainty
  • Has a corrections policy and uses it
  • Uses original sources when possible
Before You Share

The Reader's Checklist

You do not need to memorize everything in this guide. You just need a habit. Run through these before you believe or share:

  • Do I know who made this?
  • Is it fact, opinion, analysis, or advertising?
  • What is the evidence, and is it original?
  • Is the date clear? Is the location clear?
  • Are images or videos shown in their real context?
  • Are other reliable sources saying the same thing?
  • Is the headline more dramatic than the facts?
  • Am I sharing because it is true, or because it makes me feel something?
The safest reader is not the most cynical reader who doubts everything. The safest reader is the one who slows down, checks sources, looks for evidence, and asks what kind of message they are reading.
The Final Edition

Prove You Can
Read the Room

Ten questions. Pick an answer to lock it in and see the explanation. Your score updates at the bottom. There is no time limit, so think it through like a real investigator.

Question 1
"The library renovation cost $4 million, a shameful waste of money." The fact here is the cost. What is the rest?
Correct. The cost is checkable. "Shameful waste" is a judgment glued onto it.
"Shameful waste" is a judgment, not a checkable fact. Only the dollar amount is factual.
Question 2
A post has a real photo but claims it shows "your town, today." The photo turns out to be from another city three years ago. This is an example of:
Right. The asset (the photo) is real, but the claim attached to it is false. Always ask if an image is being used honestly.
The photo is real, so it is not totally fake. The problem is the false context: wrong place, wrong time.
Question 3
On the verification ladder, which is the STRONGEST evidence that a bridge closed?
Correct. Multiple independent sources plus original evidence sit at the top of the ladder.
Rumors and screenshots are low rungs. The strongest evidence is multiple independent sources confirming with original evidence.
Question 4
In SIFT, the "I" stands for Investigate the source. What question does it ask?
Yes. Investigating the source means finding out who is behind the message before trusting it.
That is the "Investigate the source" move: figuring out who made it and what others say about them.
Question 5
Lateral reading means:
Correct. You leave the page and check what other sources say, because a slick design can fool you.
Lateral reading is leaving the page to check other sources. Staying on one site and trusting its own About page is the weaker "vertical" approach.
Question 6
A cable host you disagree with AND a cable host you agree with both spend an hour telling you how to feel about the news. The smartest takeaway is:
Exactly. Strong framing is not a "one side" problem. Your job stays the same regardless of who is talking.
Be careful. It is tempting to see bias only in the side you dislike, but opinion framing appears across the spectrum. Find the facts and decide for yourself.
Question 7
A news outlet publishes a correction admitting it got a detail wrong last week. This is:
Right. Correcting the record is a sign of a trustworthy process. A source that never admits error is more worrying.
Corrections are actually a good sign. They show the outlet takes accuracy seriously and fixes mistakes.
Question 8
"Spain Guilty!" ran in giant type in 1898 before the cause of the Maine explosion was known. This is a classic example of:
Correct. Yellow journalism used sensational headlines and printed verdicts before the facts were settled.
That headline declared a verdict before any investigation finished. That sensational, evidence-light style is yellow journalism.
Question 9
The difference between misinformation and disinformation is mostly about:
Yes. Both can be false, but disinformation is deliberate while misinformation may be an honest mistake.
It is about intent. Disinformation is spread on purpose to deceive. Misinformation is often shared by someone who simply believes it.
Question 10
An article looks normal but carries a small "Sponsored" label. Before reading it as straight news, you should remember it is:
Correct. The "Sponsored" tag means its real purpose is to promote something. Read it as an ad.
The "Sponsored" label is the giveaway. Its job is to sell, even when it is shaped like a story.
